statement: The system shall gather environmental and road-condition observations from many transportation networks.
The system shall clean and quality-control the collected data.
The system shall make the data available quickly in a shared form for operational use and analysis.
The system shall improve road safety.
The system shall support better weather-related and pavement-related forecasting and response decisions.
The system shall support transportation agencies as both contributors and users of the data.
The system shall support observation-system operators as providers of sensor data and maintainers of the observation systems.
The system shall support weather-service providers as consumers who use the observations in forecasting and advisories.
The system shall support researchers as users who use the data for study and validation.
The system shall provide each stakeholder group with access appropriate to its role.
The system shall make the data broadly usable across the supported communities.

The system shall exclude sources that are not tied to environmental or road-condition observations or that cannot be reliably quality-controlled and shared in a standard way, subject to FHWA team verification.
Clarus shall ingest observations from multiple agencies and systems.
Clarus shall handle different data formats and update rates during ingestion.
Clarus shall store observations in a managed central repository.
Clarus shall retain enough history for operational review and research.
Clarus shall support timely retrieval of the latest conditions for operational users.
Clarus shall provide alerting or notification to operational users when important thresholds or weather-related changes occur.
Clarus shall support search by location for analysis users.
Clarus shall support search by time for analysis users.
Clarus shall support search by sensor type for analysis users.
Clarus shall support search by condition for analysis users.
Clarus shall allow analysis users to find and compare observations over time.
When feeds arrive in bursts or at different rates, the system shall favor timely delivery of the latest trusted data rather than waiting for perfect completeness.
For some uses, a delay of a few minutes may be acceptable.
For active weather response, the system shall provide data as close to real time as the source systems can support.
The system shall buffer incoming data so short bursts do not overwhelm ingestion.
The system shall not drop older records if they are still needed for history or validation.
The system shall queue older records for later processing when they are within a reasonable retention window.
The system shall apply back-pressure or throttling when a source is flooding the system so one feed does not degrade the whole platform.
The Clarus Weather System shall support collecting transportation weather and road-condition observations.
The Clarus Weather System shall support interactions with different users and agencies.
The system shall support transportation operations.
The system shall support the needs of FHWA.
The system shall support the needs of agencies and partners who contribute to observations.
The system shall support the needs of agencies and partners who use observations.
Clarus shall bring together environmental and road-condition observations from transportation networks into one integrated system.
Clarus shall make the data available to transportation agencies, observation-system operators, weather-service providers, and researchers.
Clarus shall support road safety improvement.
Clarus shall support faster weather response.
Clarus shall support better forecasting.

Data shall be collected through station systems.
Data shall be collected through weather-related sources operated by different agencies or vendors.

Checks and formats shall be consistent across all sources.
Sharing shall happen through different channels and interfaces.
The system shall support combining observations quickly and using them in a unified way.
The system shall provide one consistent pipeline for bringing in observations.
The system shall reduce manual reconciliation between sources.
The system shall make data available to operational users more timely.
The system shall make it easier for researchers and weather providers to access the same trusted dataset without each group building separate integrations.
The system shall support different access levels for different users.
The system shall provide different ways to retrieve data for different users.
The system shall treat operationally sensitive information as requiring controlled publication.
The system shall grant agencies and operators broader access for contribution and monitoring.
The system shall provide researchers and weather providers primarily with read access or standardized feeds.
The system shall provide reporting and visibility into data quality.
The system shall provide reporting and visibility into source status.
The system shall provide reporting and visibility into outages.
The system shall support strong metadata.
The system shall provide alerting for missing data.
The system shall provide alerting for suspect data.
The system shall vary access and distribution methods by user type.
Clarus shall prioritize timely availability.
The system shall ingest observations from multiple transportation and weather-related sources without requiring each source to have a completely custom treatment.
The system shall support source-based checks that treat certain feeds differently based on their reliability or known issues.
Clarus shall provide people with a trusted shared picture of current road and weather conditions.
Clarus shall support better decision-making during daily operations.
Clarus shall address the problem that information is scattered across different agencies and systems.
Clarus shall provide operators with a timely and consistent view of what is happening on the roadway.
People shall be able to rely on Clarus during winter storms.
Clarus shall be useful for routine monitoring.
Clarus shall support planning maintenance or treatments when crews need to know what conditions are actually on the ground.
The system shall help agencies respond sooner and more accurately to dangerous road conditions.
The system shall support better decisions on treatments when weather conditions start to deteriorate.
The system shall improve the quality of information available to weather-service providers and researchers.
The system shall distinguish between a raw observation, a quality-controlled observation, and a derived condition or alert.
The system shall have rules to prevent mixing unlike data or presenting data as comparable when it is not.
If a measurement is missing or inconsistent, Clarus shall preserve that status instead of forcing a value.
The system shall normalize units where possible.
The system shall support reuse of observation history to see trends over time.
The system shall support reuse of stored observations and derived products for forecasting.
The system shall make stored data available later in a form that can be trusted for comparison.
The retention period must be set with the program owners.
The system shall handle a steady, fairly high stream of observations from many agencies and sensor sites.
The system shall be reliably available for daily operations and event response.
Credentials must be protected when agencies or vendors are sending data into Clarus.

Access must be limited to the appropriate roles at the points where agencies or vendors send data, users access operational dashboards or downloads, and administrative changes are made to sources or quality-control settings.
Sensitive data must be protected when feeds include information not meant for broad distribution.
The system shall keep audit logs for important operational and security actions.
Observation collection varies by agency and by sensor type.
Some observations are collected automatically from roadway and weather sensors and pushed to downstream systems.
Clarus shall accommodate multiple handoff points for incoming data.
Clarus shall fail gracefully during a handoff problem or interruption.
Clarus shall provide enough visibility for operators to identify where the break occurred.
The system shall include enough information to identify the source of an observation record.

If the source method differs in a way that could change interpretation, Clarus shall preserve the original value and mark the data as not directly comparable.
Clarus should detect overlapping report periods and either reconcile the overlap according to source rules or flag it for review.
Clarus should not treat duplicate or conflicting records as separate truth.

Clarus shall include pavement conditions as an in-scope observation type.
Clarus shall include visibility as an in-scope observation type.
Clarus shall include precipitation as an in-scope observation type.
Clarus shall include wind as an in-scope observation type.
Clarus shall include temperature as an in-scope observation type.

Clarus shall include weather-service providers as contributors in scope.
Clarus shall include researchers as contributors in scope.
Clarus shall prioritize contributors whose data supports road safety and forecasting.

Clarus shall assume nationwide flexibility rather than being limited to a single jurisdiction or road class.
Clarus shall integrate observations wherever they exist.
Researchers shall provide clear provenance for their observations.
Researchers shall provide the methods used to produce their observations.
Researchers shall provide any known limitations of their observations so Clarus can judge whether the data is appropriate for operational use.

The system shall treat data as successful when it is timely, usable, traceable, and trusted enough by operational users to support decisions.
The system shall allow contributors to send data consistently.
The system shall be considered working when the core observation flow is stable and the main stakeholder groups can use it without a lot of manual intervention.
If source rules conflict with Clarus policy, Clarus policy should prevail.
When source rules conflict with Clarus policy, the source’s claim should be recorded for traceability rather than automatically accepted.
If more than one source claims precedence, Clarus should not guess.
If a deterministic tie-break rule has been approved, Clarus should apply that rule when more than one source claims precedence.
If no approved deterministic tie-break rule exists, Clarus should route the conflict for manual resolution or leave it marked unresolved until the conflict is cleared.
Follow-up action shall be triggered when issues start affecting trust or operational usefulness.
Poor integration shall trigger action when it causes delays.
Some recurring issues may be tolerated temporarily if the source is still providing unique value and the problems are clearly documented.
Known problems shall not become the permanent state.
Clarus shall comply with the usual federal data handling expectations that apply to a government system.
Clarus shall follow transportation-domain practices for sharing operational observations.
The specific regulations that FHWA treats as mandatory for this program must be verified.
Clarus shall maintain data integrity.
Logs tied to a security incident shall be retained longer than routine operational logs.
Logs tied to a security incident shall be restricted more tightly than routine operational logs.
Records containing sensitive source details shall be excluded from normal visibility.
Sensitive logs shall be handled separately from routine logs.
If an interruption is brief and Clarus can safely hold incoming observations without overflow or data loss, the system shall keep buffering incoming observations.
If an outage is longer or the backlog starts to threaten capacity, the system shall switch into a controlled recovery mode.
The system shall prioritize protecting critical observations first and avoiding silent loss.
Clarus shall accept observations at whatever handoff point the contributor can support reliably.
Clarus should avoid setups that create unnecessary manual handling or make it hard to determine the data source or whether the data was altered.
In deployments where data quality is a bigger concern, a staging or validation step may be worth the extra complexity.
Clarus shall preserve the original source and unique record ID exactly as received so the record can always be traced back.
If a value is corrected during validation, the system shall keep both the original and corrected versions along with who or what made the change and when it happened.
For time, location, observation type, and any site or sensor ID, Clarus shall carry these values forward unless they are clearly wrong or missing.
Clarus shall replace time, location, observation type, and any site or sensor ID only through an auditable correction process when they are clearly wrong or missing.
Any corrected identifiers shall remain linked to the original observation so the chain of custody is preserved.
A research observation that has been checked against Clarus quality rules and for which the source and method are reasonably clear can be labeled as usable for operations.
If the method or quality of a research observation cannot be fully verified, the system should still accept it but mark it as informational or experimental.
If provenance is incomplete, the system should make that uncertainty visible rather than hidden.
Clarus should usually accept an observation and flag it rather than reject it outright.
Clarus should reject an observation if the value is clearly invalid, such as having a bad format or being a physically impossible reading.
If an observation came from a research source and has not been vetted to the same standard as an operational feed, the system should explicitly mark it as research-only or experimental.
The system should treat an observation as operationally usable only when the source, method, and quality controls are known and it has passed the validation Clarus applies for routine use.
To avoid confusion, the record should show the source type, collection method if known, validation status, and any limitations or caveats.
The system should apply restrictions to observation data when a contributor has licensing terms, security concerns, or privacy-related limits attached to the data.
Clarus should honor contributor conditions and only share an observation with users or partners who are allowed to receive it under the contributor’s agreement.
If an observation has no special restriction, the default sharing mode should be broad sharing for transportation and research use.
Clarus shall carry observation restriction metadata forward wherever the observation goes, including edits, history records, exports, and derivative products.
If a derived product includes restricted source data, the restriction shall propagate to the output unless the contributor’s terms explicitly allow broader reuse.
If Clarus cannot guarantee that a history entry or export will honor a sharing limit, it shall not produce that output in a way that exposes the restricted content.
Clarus may narrow sharing only if a later validation or governance rule identifies a problem with the record.
Clarus shall treat credentials, internal system details, and sensitive operational data as restricted.
Clarus shall log access to restricted information carefully.
Clarus shall handle boundary cases such as test environments, incident response, and authorized administrative access under tighter controls and audit logging.
Clarus shall follow applicable privacy, cybersecurity, and federal records requirements for FHWA-connected systems.
Clarus shall base viewing and sharing decisions on role, authorization, and whether the person is acting under an approved operational purpose.
Restricted observations shall only be visible to users with an explicit need to know.
Sharing restricted observations outside the explicit-need-to-know group shall be blocked unless a designated authority has approved it.
Output from test, incident-response, or administrative contexts shall not be released to normal downstream users unless it has been reviewed, sanitized, and reclassified as safe for general release.
Audit details shall be treated as sensitive by default and shown only to authorized staff for a specific non-routine purpose.
If audit details are exported, the export shall be limited to the minimum needed and protected the same way as the original logs.
Only people or systems with an approved need for the export should receive it.
An emergency or exception path should be allowed only if there is a documented incident or legal obligation and an authorized approver signs off.
Clarus shall treat the sharing restriction as part of the data itself rather than as separate paperwork.

If a downstream system combines restricted data with less restricted data, the combined result shall inherit the stricter rule unless the restricted portion has been removed or explicitly reapproved for broader sharing.
Search and visualization must respect the same access restrictions as the underlying observations.
The system should allow filtering by observation type, source, location, time range, confidence, and quality status.
The system must clearly indicate when a result is estimated, stale, incomplete, or flagged by quality control.
The interface should not present low-confidence or unverified data as confirmed ground truth.
Aggregated or derived views should be labeled so users understand they are interpreting a summary rather than a raw observation.
If the user needs the raw observation, Clarus shall provide a clear drill-down path from the summary to the source record, provided the user is authorized to see it.
If the source record is missing or unavailable, Clarus shall show a clear message stating that the raw observation cannot be retrieved right now and, if known, provide the reason.
If the source record is archived, Clarus shall route the user to the archive only if the user is allowed to access it there.
If the source record is temporarily unavailable, Clarus shall let the user retry later.
A missing, archived, or temporarily unavailable source record should remain reachable from the summary for as long as that summary or derived view is retained.
The system should open the raw record only when it is actually available and the user is permitted to access it.
The summary may remain available if it is still valid.

The system shall enforce a limit on how long a summary or derived view can keep pointing to a missing, archived, or temporarily unavailable source record, and that limit shall be tied to the program's retention and legal-hold rules.
If the raw record was accessed under different permission rules, Clarus shall not continue exposing a path that bypasses the current rules.
For normal use, search and map browsing should feel effectively immediate.
For normal use, typical page actions should return in a couple of seconds.
Heavier requests such as large exports or broad queries across many observations may take longer.
When heavier requests take longer, the system should provide progress feedback instead of leaving users waiting silently.
Performance targets may vary by page type and data volume.
A simple record view should be much faster than a national-scale search or a complex derived dataset.
The system should set stricter targets for common interactive pages than for bulk or analytical pages.
For the main search and map pages, the system should display initial results and map markers in about 2 to 3 seconds for a typical query.
Simple detail views should load in about 1 to 2 seconds.
For larger data volumes, the system's responsiveness target may be relaxed, but the system should remain usable.
For broad searches over a large region or long time range, the system should return partial results or incremental updates instead of waiting to show anything until all results are ready.
Day-to-day upkeep shall be owned by the operations or support team.
The program team shall retain ownership of policy decisions.
The program team shall retain ownership of major changes.
For vendor-hosted pieces or external data feeds, some ownership may be shared.
Operations should handle routine incidents such as a failed feed.
Operations should handle routine incidents first if they can resolve them without changing business rules or data governance.
Issues that affect the meaning of the data should be escalated to the program team or the relevant owner.
Issues that impact public-facing availability should be escalated quickly.
Operations should handle restoration and triage.
The support team shall handle routine security operations, including account provisioning, password resets, certificate renewal, monitoring, patching, and responding to alerts.
Any change to access policy, credential scope, sharing rules, or the sensitive data that can be collected or exposed shall require program team approval or oversight.
Adding, removing, or materially changing a contributor system connection shall involve the program team or the data owner.
The support team may execute operational mechanics, but the program team shall govern the rules and approve exceptions.
The system shall support immediate escalation when an incident could corrupt or misrepresent observations.
A temporary workaround shall not be considered sufficient when an issue changes the integrity or meaning of the data.
A temporary workaround shall not be considered sufficient when an issue could cause users to make a bad operational decision.
Operations shall escalate a problem right away when the problem requires a policy exception.
Clarus should become the system of record for an area as soon as the migrated data and integrations for that area are validated.
Legacy processes should remain available briefly as a fallback during cutover.
For processes that affect shared data or reporting, there should be a clear cutoff date approved by the program team to prevent indefinite updates in two systems.
The system shall allow switching back to the legacy process only if Clarus has a serious outage.
If the issue is limited and can be patched quickly, operations shall use a temporary workaround instead of switching back to the legacy process.
Fallback to the legacy process is justified if users would otherwise be making decisions on bad or incomplete data.
The decision to fallback to the legacy process shall be approved by the program lead or the designated business owner.
Operations shall recommend the fallback decision based on the incident.
For anything broader than a local issue, the affected agency or data owner shall be included in the loop before the fallback path is declared active.
Immediate fallback is justified when Clarus is unavailable.
If the problem is affecting safety-related operations or multiple users at once, that is sufficient evidence to move fast rather than wait.
In a true emergency, the program lead or business owner can approve the switch before notifying the affected agency or data owner.

The system shall support historical data access for research.
